utterances.text: Taking the road from Bijeljina to Amajlije you go straight, and Popovi you turn left. But they're not far from each other, they're quite near.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Our map is inadequate for these purposes. You've told us of the Serbs gathering at Amajlije. Was there any particular reason why that village was chosen for them, or by them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a short distance from Serbia, and they were getting assistance to attack Bijeljina from there. So across the river is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the detention centre at Amajlije yourself or were you simply told about it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims couldn't go there of late. People talked about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's been put to you that you were registered by the Red Cross. You've said you were registered or first registered at Doboj. The list that we've produced purports -- is said to be a list from the time of your second stay at Batkovic. Having been registered at Doboj, did you remain a registered prisoner during your second stay at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the Red Cross does the registering, wherever you're hiding, you're protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness -- can the Court view from the overhead projector, if it doesn't have it already, a couple of passages from the Reuters report on the visit to the Batkovic camp, and I'll read out the entries for the witness to follow. I've forgotten or failed to record the number. 115, Defence Exhibit 115. I'm grateful to Ms. Wee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had put to you by the accused certain passages of a report from an international newspaper report provided by Reuters. On the first page, towards the bottom of the page, the report says this, that the president of the Serb commission, Major Savic, described Batkovic as a "... collection centre for Muslims and Croats who in any way participated in combat activities or collecting weapons and ammunitions." Was it true to suggest to the newspaper that everyone in Batkovic had been in some way involved in combat activities or was that false?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a blatant lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that question to the degree that's requested by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't follow that. I've asked the question whether the content of material in this report is accurate, and rather, as he's already said in his examination-in-chief, this passage would seem to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can speak of his knowledge of the camp as he's dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question is in any way participated in combat activities or collecting weapons and ammunition of the whole of -- the entire people within the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter of weight, isn't it? He deals with the people he knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remind us again, how many hundreds or more people were there in this camp when you first went to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were close to 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second page of the report, please, Usher. About a third of the way down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage that was put to you in part by the accused, it was suggested to the newspaper reporter that at Batkovic, "Prisoners get the same army rations three times a day as the Serb soldiers and military police who guard them." And then the second sentence is: "There is no obvious rancor between prisoners and Serbs and the International Red Cross visits every week." Was it true as reported, that you were getting army rations the same as the Serb soldiers and military police?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beans, the same beans. Now, whether they ate these beans, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it been sauerkraut, that might have been better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is suggested further down the page that most men were talkative to the reporter. When reporters came to the camp, so far as you were aware -- when reporters came to the camp, were you allowed to talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were hidden away, the ten of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back, did you discover one way or another whether the other prisoners were allowed to speak freely to the reporters or not or don't you know? Were they allowed to speak freely to the reporters? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. I know for my -- I can speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then just two more passages from this report. Immediately following on the same page, or one paragraph dividing, then this passage, the deputy commander or commandant, Mlado Zastavnik, was said to have "... contradicted Savic, saying that 85 per cent of the camp's inmates were harmless." Did you know the man Mlado Zastavnik?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the camp, yes. I didn't know him before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we turn over the page to the last entry I'd like you to comment on. The newspaper report includes this passage, Mr. Gusalic, that "Zastavnik said we can't leave them outside because Muslims or Croats would be shot by Serb extremists if they were left in the streets of the town." Were you aware one way or another of your being kept prisoner to save you from extremists of that kind, Serb extremists in the town?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wouldn't have beaten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And then two other questions and I'm done. You were asked about blockading of the town, and I think of the hospital. When you were first in the hospital, were there any Serbs there being treated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were. There were Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any question of Serbs being barred by roadblocks or otherwise from getting to the hospital for treatment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question about your state of memory. You've explained to the Judges that in fact of these events you have a good and strong memory. Do you suffer -- you told us something of your suffering. Do you suffer in the night from recollection of these events from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nights are difficult. That's true. That's normal. But -- and of course I remember everything very well. They haven't managed to do away with my memory yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusalic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While the witness is leaving, we'll deal with the exhibits. Let me return that to the registry. We will consider 114, which the rapporteur's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I add one point which I understated? Although produced as Rule 68, the accused had only had two pages. He had on an earlier occasion been provided with the full report, it being then intended and may be still intended that it should be an exhibit in the case, but that decision has yet to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've read it. We bear in mind what you say about it but it seems to be right to admit it. Exhibit D114. We will do that. You asked about the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need that. Thank you. One other matter. I take it the witness is being collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He is a witness with protection, and we will have to arrange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Well, before we do, procedural matters. If on Thursday we've got the hearing, the videolink, tomorrow we should deal with the procedural matters, it seems. We're not sitting on Friday, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There are -- it did seem sensible to me that perhaps tomorrow, after this next witness, might be a convenient time to raise procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will -- tomorrow is Wednesday, isn't it? That will leave the balance of tomorrow and the balance of Thursday for the fourth witness for the week, assuming there is some time. Mr. Groome reminds me that that witness who has yet to travel -- is travelling now is on his third trip here because of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must try and get through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Must try and get through him. The next witness is comparatively short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next witness is fairly short. The procedural matters can be dealt with fairly shortly, I hope. No more than one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. It's a question I think of outlining our concerns and our request to the Court and possibly giving notification of applications that we'll make so that we can tidy things up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is that aspect of it. Of course no one is to be hurried. There is also the 92 bis witnesses, which will take a bit of time, but I would hope we can deal with it in one session. But what we'll aim to do then is to deal with that after this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we make arrangements for this witness to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to raise two procedural matters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be convenient if you would do that tomorrow. We've got this witness coming in. We'll set aside some time tomorrow, as I've said, to deal with procedural matters. It may be convenient to deal with them together then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be concerned, of course, if there was anything in the procedural problems of the accused that would deal with Thursday's hearing, but I assume from the observations he made yesterday that he is as anxious as we are that Thursday's witness can be heard and dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever happens, Thursday's witness will be heard, provided that the arrangements can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look, please, at this piece of paper. Tell us, please, just yes or no, is that your correct name and your correct date of birth? Did you hear me? Is that your correct name and correct date of birth? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could that piece of paper be exhibited, the witness to be known as B-071. There will be limited number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 415 under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the remaining exhibits, therefore, be given a number. I forecast it might be Exhibit 416, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 416.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of those have redacted versions for display, as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-071, are you a Croat by ethnicity, born in Jajce in Bosnia-Herzegovina, doing mandatory military service, working in construction thereafter, someone who was never politically active?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the Territorial Defence, and did you work as a courier --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and perform reconnaissance missions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time was the Territorial Defence for which you were serving functioning as a protection unit in the area where it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: It wasn't a protection unit. It was TO defence. It acted in defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In March of 1992, was there distribution of Territorial Defence weapons to local Croats and did you receive a pistol at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of May of 1992, were you sent to Bijelajci in the area of Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that the Chamber would now be assisted by a map. So this is part of 336, to be 336B/71A, as I understand. May it be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a look at this map, if you would be so good. You're familiar with maps, B-071?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, if we can find Mrkonjic Grad on this map, please. Can you point it out to us, please. It is the wrong map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Better have this map instead, please. My error. Very well. Thank you very much. We can see at the bottom of this map, circled by you with a cross, we can see Mrkonjic Grad, and is that the area to which you were sent in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to the Ministry of Interior building in Mrkonjic Grad and questioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken after questioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They took me back again, and from there to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was stationed at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: For a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get to Manjaca, paragraph 6, the barracks at Mrkonjic Grad were called what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept there before being sent on to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I was there between seven and ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While there, what happened to you? Were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as being questioned, were you treated in any inappropriate way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There was some mistreatment and beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How bad was the beating and with what were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They beat us with batons and cables, telephone cables or electricity cables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you injured as a result or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I still feel it when there's a change of weather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from you, what other people were detained in the Kula barracks? Croats? Any other ethnicity? What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There were Croats and Muslims or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which towns, villages, or areas did those other detainees come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There was Jajce, Gruske Dolan, Majdan, Jezerov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the days you spent at Kula and again before getting to Manjaca prison, did you go first to Bijelajci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you detained there, this being, I think, a former dairy farm? Where were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They held us there in a room where the livestock was kept. Stables, sheds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many detainees were there there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Some 30-odd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the area securely fenced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. There was quite a large fence of between two and a half and three metres in height.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By what force were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police from where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: From the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you obliged when there to do any work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: For example, we went to the frontline. We dug trenches. We carried their dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the guard of whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police that you describe, what insignia or uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms and the insignia of the army of Republika Srpska, and some had JNA patches written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about the colour of their belts or the colour of the belts in any event of some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: White belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the VRS soldiers have particular flags on their caps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They had the tricolour flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While working on the frontline, were you or any of the other detainees injured or possibly, even worse, killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There were some dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it following this period of time that you moved to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put a month in the year of 1992 when you moved to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: It was sometime in mid-June or July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On transfer, by what national, by what ethnic and by what geographical group were you taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I was taken there by the military police of the Banja Luka or Krajina Corps, and they were Serbs by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Manjaca, were there two groups of prisoners dealt with in different ways, the one of which you were a part being kept separate and having no duties at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did other prisoners -- were other prisoners kept separately in a barn, Manjaca also having been a farm before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the prisoners from that barn in the exercise yard, and if so, what did you notice about their appearance and condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They appeared to have been beaten up. They didn't have enough food. They were dirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as they walked in the exercise yard, what did they have to do with their hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They held them above their heads, behind their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your time at Manjaca, did you hear noises indicating what was happening to other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. One could hear shouting and -- as they yelled at the prisoners, how they threatened to kill them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular cell you had to clean from time to time? If so, what did you notice of what was in it on its walls and floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed quite a lot of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you have to clean the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Well, let's say twice a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Well, let's say at noon and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but for how many weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: For about a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there always blood there, fresh blood, or was it something that only happened from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Whenever I cleaned that room, there was blood in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who -- which force was in charge of Manjaca prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I only remember the nickname Spaga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the individual. What force, what type of soldier or policeman was in charge of the camp as you could understand it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The military police. That same force from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you moved from Manjaca to another camp, the Prnjavor camp called Stari Mlin in Vijaka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you move there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there direct or did you go there via another town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I was first in Banja Luka in the Mali Logor, and then from there they transferred me to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say about your own ethnicity in order to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I said that I was the child of a mixed marriage, that I was half Croat, half Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was indeed that a position you were to take for some considerable period of time in order to protect yourself, as we shall see from the rest of your account?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Prnjavor in the Stari Mlin camp, who was in charge? What group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The Wolves of Veljko Milankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men constituting these Wolves were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There may have been about 300 of them that I saw in the compound of that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that they were described as the Wolves of Veljko Milankovic, but in fact were they also known as the Wolves of some other name, perhaps a shorter name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do, come back to it, or I may in due course ask you about it if it's covered in your statement. The -- this camp, then, was a camp of armed men. Was it a detention camp or were you simply being kept there in some way to work with the soldiers, with a measure of freedom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There was a room where I had to work. It wasn't a real camp with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person there in your capacity or were there others in a similar capacity to yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There were others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I had the SMB uniform without any insignia, without shoelaces, without a belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of tasks did you perform while at this Stari Mlin camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I cut wood for the soldiers, I cleaned the compound and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do other domestic chores; making coffee, washing dishes, things of that sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: No, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to travel with any part of the armed Wolves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far would you go with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: For instance, from Prnjavor to Vlasenica. I don't know what the distance is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would be the purpose of your travelling with them when they made that journey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I carried food for them. Sometimes I would dig trenches or dugouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which part of the Wolves was it that were travelling on this occasion? Was it just a general part of them or was it a special group or platoon that was travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: They were some kind of an Intervention Platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having what particular functions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: To hold the frontline and to prevent any breakthrough in the line being made by Bosniaks or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Wolves Intervention Platoon acting in this way, did it act in combination with another group that you got to know of, coming from Derventa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There was a group called Vitezovi, or the Knights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They worked together with the Wolves, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The patch displayed on the screen in front of you - it appears, I hope - do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I would see this patch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That being the patch of which group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 349, tab 9. In 1993 and possibly between 1993 and into 1994, were you sufficiently established in your position as a person working for the Wolves that you were able to apply for a transfer to Derventa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a VRS military barracks there, Zdravko Pcelar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll sort out the maps tomorrow so I don't waste any time by producing the wrong one again. And I'll deal with them comprehensively tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you want to go to Derventa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Well, actually, to get acquainted with the enemy army and to see the crimes they were committing and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was your purpose in going there, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was your stated purpose to the superiors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything you knew about the distribution of Croats in the area of Derventa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Zdravko Pcelar, who was the barracks commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I remember Major Slavko Lisica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the scope of his command? What was included in his command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: The entire Derventa Brigade, the 327th, all of the units of the army of Republika Srpska in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That man, do you know what position he holds now, Slavko Lisica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Just now I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While at this barracks, did you see visits made by senior military figures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Name those who you saw visit, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I saw Talic, for instance. There were other officers, but I can't remember. Bosko Pajovic, a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any others at the level of Talic that you can remember? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: There were some, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that again later, probably tomorrow. In these barracks, did you continue in the tasks of one kind or another for the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include domestic tasks involving food and washing dishes and matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move out of the barracks into the area of the town of Derventa itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to leave Derventa altogether or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any identification or travel papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there checkpoints around Derventa where you would have had to produce such papers had you wished to escape altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Yes. For example, you'd be stopped by the military police. You had to say where you worked, and if they were suspicious, you would be taken back to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you regard yourself then? And I'll try and let you put it in your own words: How did you regard yourself when at this camp in terms of either a free person working for an army or the other extreme, somebody who was completely a detainee? How did you regard yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: I regarded myself as a free person. I was able to move around. I was able to get food regularly and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in any sense a volunteer for what you were doing or were you obliged to be doing what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-071
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I was obliged to. That was the only way I could survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time. Witness B-071, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Could you remember in this adjournment and any others there may be not to speak to anybody until your evidence is over about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
